title: 2 Samuel 24:1–9
context: Again the LORD’s anger burns against Israel, and he moves David to count Israel and Judah; Joab objects but is overruled, and the census takes nearly ten months. The parallel in 1 Chronicles 21:1 says Satan moved David, and readers in both traditions hold the two accounts together rather than ignoring the tension. Both traditions affirm that God is just and not the author of sin and that David was responsible, while describing God’s role in different terms. The same question of how God’s agency relates to evil agents is treated as a key contrast at Judges 9:23.

verses.text: Again the LORD’s anger burned against Israel, and he moved David against them, saying, “Go, count Israel and Judah.”
verses.arminianNotes:
“Again the LORD’s anger burned against Israel, and he moved David against them.” Arminian readers usually read this as God, in judicial anger at Israel’s sin, permitting Satan’s agency (1 Chr 21:1) and giving David over to a desire already in his heart (cf. James 1:13).

The reason for God’s anger is not stated, and “again” may look back to 21:1.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers hold the two accounts together by affirming that God governs all events, including Satan’s activity, so that 1 Chronicles 21:1 names the secondary agent and 2 Samuel 24:1 the ultimate sovereign (cf. Job 1–2; 1 Kings 22:19–23).

They affirm that God is not the author of sin and that David alone bears the guilt (v. 10).

verses.text: The king said to Joab the captain of the army, who was with him, “Now go back and forth through all the tribes of Israel, from Dan even to Beersheba, and count the people, that I may know the sum of the people.”
verses.arminianNotes:
David orders Joab to count the people from Dan to Beersheba. Arminian readers note that the motive is not stated, though many suspect pride or trust in military strength (cf. Ps 20:7).

Censuses were not wrong in themselves (Num 1:2).
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also note the unstated motive. Exodus 30:12 required a ransom when Israel was counted, and some connect the plague with that requirement.

Both traditions treat the exact sin as debated.

verses.text: Joab said to the king, “Now may the LORD your God add to the people, however many they may be, one hundred times; and may the eyes of my lord the king see it. But why does my lord the king delight in this thing?”
verses.arminianNotes:
Joab wishes the people multiplied a hundredfold but asks why the king delights in this. Arminian readers note that even Joab sensed something wrong.

His objection implies a spiritual problem.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see Joab’s question as exposing David’s motives, even though Joab himself was no model of piety.

1 Chronicles 21:3 adds Joab’s question about why David would bring guilt on Israel.

verses.text: Notwithstanding, the king’s word prevailed against Joab and against the captains of the army. Joab and the captains of the army went out from the presence of the king to count the people of Israel.
verses.arminianNotes:
The king’s word prevails, and Joab and the captains go out to count. Arminian readers note that David overrode wise counsel.

Authority used against good advice leads to harm.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see David’s responsibility for insisting on the census.

The narrative assigns the decision clearly to David.

verses.text: They passed over the Jordan and encamped in Aroer, on the right side of the city that is in the middle of the valley of Gad, and to Jazer;
verses.arminianNotes:
They cross the Jordan and camp at Aroer and toward Jazer. Arminian readers note the census route beginning in the east.

Some locations are uncertain.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see the thoroughness of the count as it begins east of the Jordan in the territory of Gad.

Both traditions note that several places on the route cannot be identified with certainty.

verses.text: then they came to Gilead and to the land of Tahtim Hodshi; and they came to Dan Jaan and around to Sidon,
verses.arminianNotes:
They go to Gilead, Tahtim Hodshi, Dan Jaan, and around to Sidon. Arminian readers note that “Tahtim Hodshi” and “Dan Jaan” are uncertain names.

The route moves north.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see the census reaching the northern edges of David’s kingdom.

Several place names here, including “Tahtim Hodshi” and “Dan Jaan,” are textually difficult, and both traditions treat them as uncertain.

verses.text: and came to the stronghold of Tyre, and to all the cities of the Hivites and of the Canaanites; and they went out to the south of Judah, at Beersheba.
verses.arminianNotes:
They reach the stronghold of Tyre and the Hivite and Canaanite cities, then Beersheba. Arminian readers note the census reaches the borders.

The route returns south.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see the circuit completed from the far north back to Beersheba in the south.

The mention of Hivite and Canaanite cities shows the mixed population within the land David ruled.

verses.text: So when they had gone back and forth through all the land, they came to Jerusalem at the end of nine months and twenty days.
verses.arminianNotes:
After nine months and twenty days they return to Jerusalem. Arminian readers note the long effort.

The census was a major undertaking.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see the long time spent on a project that God would judge, underlining David’s persistence in it.

Both traditions note that nine months gave ample time for reflection before David’s heart struck him.

verses.text: Joab gave up the sum of the counting of the people to the king; and there were in Israel eight hundred thousand valiant men who drew the sword, and the men of Judah were five hundred thousand men.
verses.arminianNotes:
Joab reports 800,000 in Israel and 500,000 in Judah. Arminian readers note that 1 Chronicles 21:5 gives different figures.

The numbers are a textual issue interpreters discuss.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also note the variant numbers in 1 Chronicles 21:5–6, which adds that Levi and Benjamin were not counted.

The differences are noted, not resolved.
